title: Sharp Practice
blurb: A queen bee, a sixty-day permit and a seventy-day haul: the Code is very particular about letters.

blocks.text: Peregrine Blott came down the ladder into the hold and found the argument already going, with Soph winning it.

"Four hull days," she was saying. "That's what she's got in a cage. Out of the hive, with a handful of attendants and a lump of sugar candy, four hull days, and then she's the most expensive dead insect on Quarto."

The queen's box sat on the hold bench between Soph's table book and Jory's elbow. It was a handsome little thing, varnished, no bigger than a paperback, with the Quarto apiary stamp burned into its lid: a bee standing on a scrap of comb. Something inside it buzzed in a small, offended way.
"Four's plenty," said Jory. "Twenty to one, we're at Hearth in three and a half. She'll have half a day to spare and a good view."
"Her export permit runs sixty days," said Soph. "On Quarto's calendar. Ground days, because it names Quarto, and Quarto doesn't care how fast we go. The haul to Hearth is seventy."
Jory considered this the way he considered a bad bearing, slowly and from several sides, and then he smiled at the box. "So she's legal for most of the trip."
"Technically she's contraband for the last ten days of it."
The buzzing went on. Peregrine looked at the box, and at the permit pinned under Soph's thumb, and at the hold clock.
"Running late," he said. "Still running."
Jory laughed before Soph could, which was the usual order of things.

It was a good job, and Peregrine wanted it done properly. An orchard on Hearth had lost its queen in a cold snap, the apple bloom was coming whether anyone was ready or not, and a Quarto queen, bred hard for Fringe winters, could carry those trees. The Drift would keep her young; hull time was the only thing in the Spread kinder to a bee than a hive. Nothing could tether her there. Nothing alive bigger than a seed came out the far side of a Turn. She had to ride, in the hold, in her box, with the heaters turned up.
"Where's Amberley?" he said.
"Ashore, settling up with the breeder," said Jory. "He's on the manifest. He'll fret the whole way to Hearth."
"He can fret," said Soph. "Fretting isn't a permit."
Nobody had said Bettina Marr's name since the counter. Jory, who had been standing at the counter, had been not saying it all morning, carefully, the way a man walks round a wet patch of deck.
"Captain," said Waybill from the bulkhead grille. "A person at the clamps is asking for you by rank."
Peregrine went up.

Constance Aubrey stood at the foot of the gangway with a kitbag over one shoulder and her Inspectorate coat buttoned to the throat. She did not smile. He had not expected her to. He had not expected her at all.
"Captain."
"Inspector."

"The terms of your probation allow me to ride along aboard this ship whenever I choose, without notice." She set the kitbag down on the gangway, one careful pace onto his side of the line. "I choose."
"We're bound for Hearth. Seventy days, ground."
"Then I shall see Hearth."
He picked up her kitbag. It was heavier than it looked, and an inspector's lamp case was strapped to its side, the long kind, made for hairlines. He carried it aboard and did not mention it.

In the hold, Jory looked up, saw who was behind him, and stopped talking. He picked up his spanner and began work on a bracket that had nothing wrong with it, and he did not tell the spanner anything at all.
Soph looked at Aubrey, then at Peregrine. "Why is she here?"
"She's entitled," said Peregrine.
"Entitled how?"
"On paper." He set the kitbag down outside the forward cabin. "Soph. Find me the mass."
Constance Aubrey had ridden in tidier ships and in worse ones, but never in one where the crew argued with the chart as if it owed them money.

She had gone to the keel locker first, before she took off her coat. The lamp showed her what she had seen at Saltpan: one hairline on the keel-ring, dead, exactly where she had left it, and nothing new beside it. She had not expected anything new. She had come aboard for what happened next, not for what had already happened.
By the time she reached the galley, the navigator had the route table spread across the board and the engineer was leaning on the other end of it.
"Direct, we buy Quarto mass at Quarto prices," Vell was saying. "And we buy a great deal of it, because somebody ran the drive into the red getting here."
"Somebody won Octavo a berth," said Ashdown, to the table.
"Somebody did. Somebody can pay for it."

Aubrey put a gloved finger on the chart, on the hub. "There is a mass depot at Gnomon, at Concordat prices. And the Ravel Desk. I should like to lodge my plates and my report in person, Captain, where no clerk can lose them in a light queue."
The captain said nothing. Ashdown rubbed his jaw. "Gnomon's the long way round, Inspector. She'd go round it all right. She just wouldn't come out the other side."
"She?"

"The queen," said Vell. "Quarto to Gnomon is the longest haul in the Spread. Three and a half hull days on its own, at twenty. Then we sit on Gnomon's clamps refuelling, and her clock doesn't stop for that, and then we hop in to Hearth. She'd be dead in her box somewhere past the hub. And her permit's gone weeks before."
"Two hours ashore," said Aubrey. "The Desk is in the academy district, beside the Board's halls. You need not leave the ship."
"I wouldn't," said Vell. "I'm not setting foot in the academy district."
"I did not ask you to, Navigator."

"Technically you'd have to. Technically somebody would have to walk you through the gate, because inspectors get lost in there. Technically nobody's obliged to go anywhere near it, and technically I'm not." She stopped. She folded the route table in half, and in half again, much smaller than it needed to be.
"Why?" said Aubrey.
"Because I don't want to."

Ashdown and the captain did not look at each other, in a way that took some effort. Neither of them asked. Aubrey filed it, beside the certificate she had read twice at Saltpan and the silence that had come after it.

Ashdown went below to see what Quarto's mass looked like close up. Vell went to price it, saying she might as well, since she could see where this was going. Then there were only the two of them in the galley, and the grille.
"Direct line," said the captain. "Twenty to one. I'll pay Quarto's price."
"Captain, the Inspectorate would prefer—"
"My ship, Inspector. Direct."
It was his ship. A ride-along carried no right to route a courier, and she had known that when she packed. Knowing it did not make it agreeable.
"Noted, and not agreed," said Aubrey.

Something happened to his face. It was very brief: a stillness, as if someone had said his name from a long way off. Then he became polite. Not courteous; polite, elaborately, the way a man is polite to a dog he has not met.

"Thank you, Inspector. Of course. You'll want the forward cabin; it holds the heat better. The hot water takes a minute to come through. If there's anything you need for your plates, please ask." He took a driver from the rack, went down to the queen's box on the hold bench, and tightened its clamp a quarter turn, very gently, though it had been tight.

Aubrey watched him do it. She had said only what she said in every office where somebody outranked her. He had done something like this at Saltpan, too, when her sergeant overruled her: looked up as if she had called him.
She could not think what she had said. She filed that as well.
Constance Aubrey woke on the first hull morning to the sound of the crew planning something that sounded very like fraud.

Before breakfast she had looked in the spool locker. Both Post spools sat in their cradles with their tags whole; nobody had moored a line at Quarto. Ashdown was in the drive space, where she was beginning to think he lived. The others were round the galley table: Vell, the captain, and the orchardist, Hollis Amberley, a big soft man from Hearth with earth still in the creases of his knuckles and a form in front of him that he plainly did not trust.
"It says 'sealed by the importer, in passage or on arrival,'" Amberley said. "On arrival's no good. She lands ten days past her permit. Your navigator says in passage might be."

"In passage is perfect," said Vell. "If you seal it aboard while we're under drive, it takes ship's reckoning. Not Hearth's date. Not the real date either, if there were such a thing, which there isn't."
"Ship's reckoning," said the captain, for Amberley, "is the date at the last port we filed at, plus hull time since."
"Quarto's date," said Vell, "plus about a day. So your declaration's postmarked a day after we left Quarto. Fifty-nine days to spare on the permit."
Amberley turned the form round on the table as if the other side might help. "And it counts from then? Even though she's not on Hearth till weeks after?"
"From the postmark," said the captain. "Once it's delivered valid at Hearth, it takes effect from when you sealed it. Your queen was declared while her permit was good."
Aubrey put down her tea. "That is sharp practice, Captain."
"It's the Code."

So she checked it against the Code, because that was what she was for. She had the wording by heart, and she said it aloud, slowly, so that everyone at the table could hear where the edges were. "An item sealed aboard a ship while it is under drive, as the keel log shows, takes ship's reckoning, but only if the sender is crew or a passenger who rode the haul on the manifest." She turned to the grille. "Waybill. Is this ship under drive?"
"Under drive since Quarto, Inspector. Keel log continuous. Ship's reckoning: Quarto, one day and two hours after filing."
"Is the orchardist on the manifest?"
"Passenger Amberley, orchardist, of Hearth. Boarded at Quarto. Riding the haul."
"And has any news reached this ship since Quarto? Anything at all?"
"None can, Inspector," said Waybill. "We are under drive."

She looked for the hole. Finding the hole was her trade, and she was good at it. A passenger who was not truly a passenger: no, he had come aboard with his luggage and his worry. Sealing after docking: no, they were a day out. Hindsight: no, nothing could reach them. A clever reading of the permit: no, the permit named Quarto's calendar and the postmark would carry Quarto's calendar. There was no hole. There was only a bee, and a man who wanted her for his apples.
"It is perfectly legal," said Aubrey. She said it the way a doctor names an illness.
Amberley signed. He sealed the declaration in its Post envelope, pressing with both thumbs.
"Sealed under drive," said Waybill. "Postmark: Postscript, ship's reckoning, Quarto calendar. Logged."
"I shall put in my report," said Aubrey, "that the bee was very well advised."

Vell laughed first, then Amberley, uncertainly, and then the captain made a small sound into his cup that might have been one. Aubrey kept her face exactly where it was. It took a moment longer than usual.
Peregrine Blott carried the queen down the gangway at Hearth himself.
"Docked, Hearth Main," Waybill had said as the clamps took. "Hull time since Quarto filing: three days, eleven hours. Grace begins." And from the box, faint and cross, the buzzing had answered it.

Hollis Amberley took the box from him at the foot of the gangway the way people take back a child. He had an orchard cart waiting on the concourse under a canvas hood. He looked in at the gauze end of the box, and whatever he saw made him shut his eyes.
"She's well," he said. "She's furious, but she's well."
"Good," said Peregrine.

At the counter the clerk took the live parcel and the declaration together. She ran the declaration's postmark through her drawer edition against the counter clock, which stood weeks later than anything on the envelope, and punched it. Then she punched the parcel. Valid, both. Entered.
"Bloom's in nine days," said Amberley. "She'll have her pick of it." He shook Peregrine's hand, and then, after some thought, Soph's. He did not try the inspector's.

Aubrey came down the gangway last, with her kitbag. "I shall be at the Inspectorate office on the concourse, Captain, sending my report to Gnomon by light. It will get there a good deal later than I would have." She watched the cart go. "My compliments to the bee."
Soph walked with Amberley as far as the gate, arguing with him about apples. Peregrine went back up the gangway and stood in front of the manifest board.

He had known since Quarto. He had heard it first at Saltpan and let himself think it was only a phrase, the kind of thing officers said to each other across desks. Then she had said it in his own galley, in his own air, with the fans running behind her, and it had not been a phrase. It had been the last line on a card from his ship's future.
He did not tell Soph. He did not go below and tell Jory, though he could hear Jory down there telling Margaret what Quarto's mass had cost them, which meant the inspector was off the ship.

Aubrey could not know. She had never heard the recording. The card sat in its cask under her own evidence seal, and she could not examine it without a warrant; the ship's record answered to a court, not to her. She would go on not knowing, and riding along when she chose, and saying what she said when she was overruled.
The board was clean. He wiped it anyway.
He did not ask Waybill to set her voice beside the fifth one. He did not need to.
"Waybill," he said. "One conversion. The recording's postmark against our reckoning. Round it."
"Ship's reckoning is Quarto's date until we file, Captain." The grille paused while it worked. "Converting the recording's postmark from Folio's calendar to Quarto's."
Peregrine kept his hand on the cloth.
"Fourteen months, Captain, by the Almanac."
In fourteen months, by the Almanac, the woman trying to arrest him would be aboard Postscript, arguing as crew.
